security_spec.violation_condition: Kernel code writes to memory via misaligned stores or stores wider than XLEN (e.g., FSD on RV32D) that straddle a PMP boundary, or issues CBO instructions crossing PMP region boundaries, and assumes that a PMP access-fault exception means no bytes were modified in the protected region.
security_spec.summary: PMP faults from misaligned/wide stores or decomposed CMOs may leave partially-visible writes in protected regions; kernel must not assume PMP faults are atomic with zero side effects

findings.finding: On RV32, when emulating an FSD (8-byte FP store) instruction that triggered a misaligned trap, the handler calls copy_to_user() at line 416 to write all 8 bytes in a single call. Since XLEN=32, copy_to_user() decomposes this into two 32-bit word writes. If the misaligned address straddles a page or PMP boundary such that the second 32-bit write faults, the first 32-bit write has already been committed to memory. The handler returns -1 on any copy_to_user() failure, and the caller (do_trap_misaligned at traps.c:230-232) signals SIGBUS — without any mechanism to detect or undo the partial write. This means bytes are written into the protected/faulting region despite the exception. This is the exact vulnerability pattern described by the RISC-V spec at machine.adoc:3571-3574.

spec_citations.excerpt: On some implementations, misaligned loads, stores, and instruction fetches may be decomposed into multiple memory operations, some of which may succeed before an access-fault exception occurs... In particular, a portion of a misaligned store that passes the PMP check may become visible, even if another portion fails the PMP check. The same behavior may manifest for stores wider than XLEN bits (e.g., the FSD instruction in RV32D), even when the store address is naturally aligned.

Failed memory operations generate an instruction, load, or store access-fault exception. Note that a single instruction may generate multiple memory operations, which may not be mutually atomic. An access-fault exception is generated if at least one memory operation generated by an instruction fails, though other memory operations generated by that instruction may succeed with visible side effects.

On some implementations, misaligned loads, stores, and instruction fetches may also be decomposed into multiple accesses, some of which may succeed before a page-fault exception occurs. In particular, a portion of a misaligned store that passes the exception check may become visible, even if another portion fails the exception check. The same behavior may manifest for stores wider than XLEN bits (e.g., the FSD instruction in RV32D), even when the store address is naturally aligned.

findings.finding: Same partial-write vulnerability as FSD for the compressed variants C.FSD and C.FSDSP on RV32. These also write 8 bytes (len=8) in a single copy_to_user() call, which decomposes into two 32-bit writes on RV32. If the address straddles a page/PMP boundary, the first half-write may succeed while the second faults.

spec_citations.excerpt: In particular, a portion of a misaligned store that passes the PMP check may become visible, even if another portion fails the PMP check. The same behavior may manifest for stores wider than XLEN bits (e.g., the FSD instruction in RV32D), even when the store address is naturally aligned.

findings.finding: On RV32 with FLD (8-byte FP load, len=8), copy_from_user() reads 8 bytes decomposed into two 32-bit reads. If the second read faults, copy_from_user returns an error, and the handler returns -1. While a load doesn't corrupt protected memory (it only reads), the partial read may have observable side-effects: the first 4 bytes are consumed but the instruction is retried or the process is killed. More critically, if the watched memory has MMIO side-effects on read (e.g., a FIFO), the partial read consumes data that is lost when the instruction fails. This is lower severity because it does not write into a protected region, but it is the same pattern.

clear_page() uses CBO.ZERO instructions operating on cache-block-sized regions (typically 64 bytes). Per the RISC-V CMO spec (cmo.adoc:327-328), if a CBO instruction's cache block spans two PMP regions with different permissions, the behavior is UNSPECIFIED. The kernel does not check whether the target page straddles a PMP boundary before issuing CBO.ZERO. In the kernel's own PMP configuration (head.S:237-240), PMP0 grants universal R/W/X access, so this is not triggerable by the kernel's PMP setup alone. However, with firmware-managed PMP where M-mode restricts kernel S-mode access to certain physical regions, a page allocation that spans a PMP boundary could cause UNSPECIFIED behavior — potentially zeroing memory in a protected region.
findings.snippet:
.Lzero_loop:
	CBO_ZERO(a0)
	add	a0, a0, a1
	CBOZ_ALT(11, "bltu a0, a2, .Lzero_loop; ret", "nop; nop")

spec_citations.excerpt: The PMP access control bits shall be the same for all physical addresses in the cache block, and if write permission is granted by the PMP access control bits, read permission shall also be granted... If the above constraints are not met, the behavior of a CBO instruction is UNSPECIFIED.

The access size for CMO instructions is equal to the size of the cache block, however in some cases that access can be decomposed into multiple memory operations. PMP checks are applied to each memory operation independently. For example a 64-byte cbo.zero that spans two 32-byte PMP regions would succeed if it was decomposed into two 32-byte memory operations... but if performed as a single 64-byte memory operation it would cause an access fault.

findings.finding: DMA cache management uses ALT_CMO_OP(CLEAN, ...) which emits CBO.CLEAN instructions. Similarly arch_dma_cache_inv() uses CBO.INVAL and arch_dma_cache_wback_inv() uses CBO.FLUSH. These CBO instructions access cache-block-sized regions. Same UNSPECIFIED-behavior risk as clear_page if a DMA buffer spans a firmware-enforced PMP boundary. A CBO.FLUSH that writes back dirty cache lines across a PMP boundary could corrupt protected memory. In practice, the kernel's own PMP grants universal access, so this requires external M-mode PMP enforcement to trigger.

findings.finding: The kernel boot sequence in M-mode configures PMP0 as NAPOT covering the full address space with R/W/X permissions, then never reconfigures PMP at runtime. This L=0 entry grants M-mode universal access and S/U-mode universal access. This is the correct behavior for a kernel that delegates PMP management to M-mode firmware (e.g., OpenSBI). The kernel does not attempt runtime PMP manipulation, which avoids introducing PMP-related bugs in kernel context-switch or hotplug paths.
findings.snippet:
la a0, .Lpmp_done
csrw CSR_TVEC, a0
li a0, -1
csrw CSR_PMPADDR0, a0
li a0, (PMP_A_NAPOT | PMP_R | PMP_W | PMP_X)
csrw CSR_PMPCFG0, a0

findings.finding: When the misaligned store is from kernel mode (user_mode(regs) is false), the handler uses memcpy() at line 419 instead of copy_to_user(). On RV32 with FSD (len=8), this memcpy writes 8 bytes decomposed into two 32-bit stores to kernel memory. If the kernel's own memory access triggers a page fault or PMP fault on the second 32-bit write, the first write has already been committed. While kernel memory is generally uniformly mapped, this could matter in edge cases like persistent memory (PMEM) DAX mappings or if kernel code operates on user-owned pages via kmap.
